summary: An informational framework outlining the issues in providing IP Integrated Services with RSVP over ATM.

eli5.summary: An overview of problems when trying to promise good service on one kind of network with rules from another.

questions: integrated services and rsvp over atm
how do rsvp and atm work together
how to manage atm virtual circuits for rsvp
what is multicast heterogeneity in rsvp over atm
subtitle: Making IP quality-of-service work over ATM networks

tldr.problem: The Internet's best-effort service does not work well for real-time traffic like voice and video. RSVP (Resource ReSerVation Protocol) lets applications request better service, but ATM networks below the IP layer have their own different QoS mechanisms that need to be coordinated.
tldr.mechanism: This framework outlines how to map RSVP's QoS requirements onto ATM's virtual circuits, manage the setup and teardown of those circuits, and handle issues like multicast heterogeneity and dynamic QoS changes.
tldr.outcome: The framework provides guidance for implementations to make RSVP and IntServ work over ATM, though it was informational rather than a standard; later RFCs provided detailed implementation requirements and guidelines.

facts.label: Main topic
facts.value: RSVP and Integrated Services over ATM

today: This RFC is Informational and remains the foundational framework document for understanding how RSVP and Integrated Services interact with ATM networks. While ATM has become less common in modern networks, the architecture and design patterns outlined here inform similar work in other technologies.

sections.title: The QoS Problem
sections.content:
The Internet began with a single class of service: best effort, where packets are handled first-come-first-served and may be dropped if congestion occurs. This works well for email, file transfer and web browsing, but real-time traffic like voice and video performs poorly over congested networks. To improve quality for real-time applications, the Internet adopted RSVP (Resource ReSerVation Protocol) and the Integrated Services model, which let applications ask the network to reserve bandwidth and latency for specific flows.

Many networks use ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) as the data link layer beneath IP. ATM has built-in quality-of-service features: it can set up virtual circuits with guaranteed bandwidth and latency. However, ATM's QoS mechanisms are different from RSVP's, creating a coordination problem.
sections.eli5: Your internet app wants a fast lane for video. RSVP is the app's way of asking for it. But below RSVP is ATM, which has its own way of creating fast lanes. They speak different languages, so you need a translator.

sections.title: RSVP and IntServ Models over ATM
sections.content:
RSVP and the Integrated Services model can operate over ATM in several ways. The RFC discusses modes and models for how to run RSVP: permanent virtual circuits (PVCs) offer reliable pre-allocated capacity but poor resource utilization; switched virtual circuits (SVCs) are set up on demand but incur signalling latency. For multicast, ATM's point-to-multipoint circuits help, but they require careful design because different receivers may ask for different QoS levels (heterogeneous receivers).

A key issue is how RSVP's receiver-oriented design (receivers ask for resources) aligns with ATM's sender-oriented design (senders set up circuits). The framework shows that this works: when RSVP reservation requests arrive at a sender, the sender can set up the necessary ATM circuits to receivers.

The RFC also discusses future ATM enhancements like heterogeneous point-to-multipoint circuits, lightweight signalling, QoS renegotiation, and label switching, which would make RSVP over ATM more efficient.
sections.eli5: ATM circuits can be permanent (always on but wasteful) or switched on demand (flexible but slow to set up). When many people want different speeds, ATM needs to be smarter. The RFC explores how to make these pieces fit together.

sections.title: Managing Virtual Circuits
sections.content:
The core problem is how to map RSVP reservations to ATM virtual circuits. One approach is one flow per VC: each RSVP reservation gets its own ATM circuit. This is simple to implement but uses many circuits and suffers from scaling problems. The alternative is flow aggregation: multiple RSVP reservations share one ATM circuit, like traffic shaping on a T-1 line. Aggregation saves circuits but adds complexity in scheduling and may waste bandwidth if reserved flows do not use all available capacity.

For multicast, the RFC outlines four models. Full heterogeneity creates a separate VC for each distinct QoS level (including best effort), allowing perfect matching of user requests but consuming more bandwidth. Limited heterogeneity uses just two VCs: one for best-effort receivers and one for QoS receivers. Homogeneous uses a single VC for all receivers, resized to the maximum request; simple but may deny service or charge users unfairly. A modified homogeneous model adds fallback best-effort VCs for receivers that cannot fit on the main QoS VC.
sections.eli5: When you reserve bandwidth, you need a virtual circuit to carry it. You can give each reservation its own circuit (simple but wasteful), or bunch them together (complex but efficient). With video conferences where some people want HD and others want basic service, you need a strategy for handling them together.

sections.title: Advanced VC Issues
sections.content:
When RSVP receivers request changes to their reservations at runtime, ATM circuits must be updated without dropping data. The default approach is to set up a new circuit with the new QoS, shift traffic to it, then tear down the old one. During setup, the old circuit stays active to prevent loss. If the new setup fails, traffic continues on the old circuit; if the new request is smaller than the old reservation, the request succeeds but the larger allocation remains (suboptimal but safe).

Another issue is receiver transitions in multicast. When adding receivers to a QoS VC, a receiving endpoint must be added to the QoS VC and removed from best-effort VCs. If the add happens first, the receiver might briefly get duplicates; if the drop happens first, it might miss data. The RFC recommends completing the add first, accepting that duplicates are acceptable during transitions.

ATM also supports short-cuts: direct virtual circuits across IP subnets. RSVP must handle asymmetric short-cuts where downstream and upstream paths differ, a case already covered by RSVP's message forwarding mechanisms.
sections.eli5: When a video conference changes from 10 people to 100, the circuit must resize without cutting off the call. Also, some paths get shortcuts—direct highways instead of going through toll booths. RSVP must handle this gracefully.

sections.title: RSVP Control Messages and Encapsulation
sections.content:
RSVP itself sends control messages (PATH and RESV) that must be carried over the ATM network. These control messages can ride on the same VCs as data, or use separate VCs. Separate VCs ensure control messages are not dropped due to data traffic exceeding its QoS contract, but cost extra circuits and setup latency. The RFC outlines strategies: mixed data and control (simple but risky), one control VC per reservation (double the circuits), multiplexed point-to-multipoint control VCs (efficient), and multiplexed point-to-point control VCs (flexible but complex).

For encapsulation, RSVP packets and IP data must be encoded over ATM. RFC 1483 defines two methods: LLC encapsulation (multiple protocols per VC) and VC-based multiplexing (one protocol per VC). Either can work as long as VCs are managed according to RSVP's needs. The QoS for control VCs should be modest—RSVP messages are infrequent (typically every 30 seconds)—to avoid rejecting VC setup due to insufficient resources.
sections.eli5: RSVP sends its own messages to set up reservations. These can travel with the data (risky if data is broken) or on their own circuits (safer but pricier). The RFC explores the tradeoffs and how to package everything for ATM.
